query: Starting from a multi-element automotive alloy catalyst containing multiple principal elements in nearly equiatomic ratios, what single intervention could overcome activity loss and durability limitations while maintaining low platinum-group-metal consumption during transient and low-temperature gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust operation, including exposure to H2O and NO and degradation associated with thermal aging or increasing mileage? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the untreated starting catalyst, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Selective surface doping with Sn or Bi on the automotive HEA catalyst will mitigate activity loss and durability limitations under transient, low-temperature gasoline or hybrid exhaust conditions while maintaining low platinum-group-metal consumption.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element automotive alloy catalyst with nearly equiatomic ratios containing Pt and other transition metals (e.g., Ni, Fe, Co, Cu) in HEA form.
generation.intervention: Introduce selective surface dopants (Sn or Bi) at controlled, low concentrations by post-synthesis surface treatment to decorate Pt sites.
generation.conditions: Transient and low-temperature gasoline/hybrid exhaust operation regimes, including exposure to water (H2O), nitric oxide (NO), and thermal aging conditions simulating increased mileage.
generation.structural_mediator: Surface Pt sites whose electronic properties are modified by adjacent Sn or Bi atoms.
generation.mechanism: Sn or Bi dopants alter the local electronic density around Pt sites, weakening the binding of poisoning intermediates (e.g., CO) and facilitating faster oxidation processes by enhancing OH adsorption, thereby reducing site poisoning and improving durability during fluctuating exhaust conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated HEA catalyst, the doped catalyst is predicted to show reduced activity loss and improved durability, with more stable performance over prolonged transient operation while still consuming low amounts of platinum-group metals.
generation.baseline: Untreated HEA catalyst that experiences performance degradation (activity loss and durability issues) under transient operation and exposure to H2O, NO, and thermal aging.
generation.boundary: This benefit is expected only under the specified low-temperature, transient automotive exhaust conditions; overly high dopant concentrations or non-selective dopant incorporation may lead to secondary phase formation that would negate the improvement.
generation.uncertainty: The precise improvement magnitude in catalytic performance and durability remains uncertain; the effect may vary with dopant concentration, dispersion, and exact operational conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA catalysts: one set with selective surface doping of Sn or Bi and one set without doping. Expose both sets to simulated automotive exhaust conditions featuring transient low-temperature operations with periodic H2O and NO exposure as well as thermal aging cycles. Monitor their catalytic performance and durability over time.
measurements: Catalytic activity (e.g., conversion rates of target pollutants) under standard exhaust gas mixtures.
Durability metrics (rate of activity decline over simulated mileage or thermal aging cycles).
Surface characterization (XPS, TEM) to confirm selective dopant location and quantify changes in Pt electronic structure.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the doped catalysts do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in activity retention and durability over the untreated control under the specified conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

As the first order of approximation, we introduced a doping Co/Ni/Bi/Sn atom onto Pt(111) surface to evaluate the individual contribution from each kind of element in HEASA-Pt (Supplementary Fig. 2). Co and Bi have been reported to promote electron transfer in catalysts, lowering the oxidation energy barrier of *CO and facilitating the MOR,. reading.lever: Introduce selective surface dopants (e.g., Sn or Bi) on the automotive HEA catalyst to modulate Pt-site electronic properties and mitigate poisoning under transient conditions.
reading.why: Doping interventions have improved anti-poisoning and durability in related Pt-based systems, suggesting promising translation to automotive exhaust applications.
